title: Bookkeeping Basics for Freelancers
subtitle: Records you can hand to a client, a bank or the BIR
summary: Bookkeeping for people who invoice their own clients. Twelve lessons on separating business money from personal money, keeping documents that prove what happened, running a plain spreadsheet you update weekly, and understanding what registering as self-employed commits you to, including the documents, forms and options that arrangement actually names.
description: You get paid, the money lands in the same account as your groceries, and four months later a client asks for a summary, or a bank asks what you earn, or you sit down to file and cannot reconstruct the year. This course builds the habit before you need it. You will put one boundary between business money and personal money, learn what each document in a freelance transaction actually proves, build a one-sheet income and expense ledger, record a payment correctly when platform fees, withholding and currency conversion shave it on the way in, and close each month in about an hour. The last chapter covers what being registered with the BIR commits a self-employed person to, described as an arrangement rather than as a set of figures, because rates, thresholds, form names and deadlines change and a number you read in a course is not a number you can file on. You finish with a deadline calendar built from sources you checked yourself, and the questions to ask a bookkeeper or an accountant when the work outgrows you. This is education, not tax or legal advice.

Evidence that an expense was business
Income and expense ledgers in a spreadsheet
BIR obligations and a deadline calendar you checked yourself
Working with a bookkeeper or an accountant

lessons.title: Who Asks for Your Records, and When
lessons.content_mdx:
# Who Asks for Your Records, and When

Reyna does virtual assistant work for three clients from a room in Bacolod. She has never kept books. Then one month arrives in which her longest-running client asks for a summary of everything she billed them last year, a landlord asks her to show what she earns, and a fourth client insists they already paid an invoice she is certain is unpaid.

None of those is an accounting question. They are the same question wearing three different shirts: can you show what happened.

One thing before the rest of this course, stated once so it does not need repeating in every lesson: every exact figure you meet here (a rate, a threshold, a due date) is one to confirm with the BIR or an accountant before you act on it, not one to file on straight from this screen. What you can rely on is the shape of things and the names of things, both of which change far less often than the numbers attached to them.

## The five people who will ask

**A client or an agency.** They are closing their own year and want a statement of what you billed them and when. They are not testing you. They need it to match their side.

**An institution.** A bank, a landlord, a lender, an embassy. Someone salaried hands over a payslip. You have no payslip, so you are asked to show income another way. What each institution accepts differs by institution and changes from year to year, so the only reliable move is to ask that institution directly what they want, and to ask early rather than in the last week. Do not take the answer from a forum thread, from a group chat, or from a friend who applied three years ago.

**The BIR, if you are registered.** Registration is chapter 4's subject, and this course refuses to guess at its details. What matters here is the shape: keeping books and being able to produce them is an obligation that sits on you rather than on an employer.

**A client who says they already paid.** This is the one that costs money directly. The argument is settled by evidence, or it is settled by whoever gives up first.

**You.** You cannot tell whether a retainer is worth keeping if you have never added up what it costs you to serve. The client who pays the least is not always the one to drop.

Five askers, five different cuts of the same underlying records. That is the argument for keeping one set that answers all of them, rather than assembling something new every time somebody asks.

## The panic week

Here is what happens instead, and it happens to careful people.

The request arrives and you have nothing. So you take a week. You open your bank history, scroll your e-wallet, dig through Messenger threads and Gmail, and rebuild the year from whatever is still reachable. Some of it is gone. Some of it is ambiguous: a transfer from a name you do not recognise, a payment that might have settled two invoices or might have settled one. You round the awkward figures. You guess at a date.

What you produce is a document you cannot defend. Ask yourself a follow-up question about any single line in it and you have no answer, because you did not know the answer when you wrote the line.

The second cost is worse. That week teaches you that bookkeeping is horrible. It is not. What is horrible is doing a year of it in one week, from memory, under a deadline, for free.

## The standard this course holds to

A record you can stand behind has three properties.

**You wrote it near the time it happened.** Not the same second. The same week is fine. March is not.

**It points at a document that exists.** A statement line, an invoice you issued, a receipt, a message where the client confirmed the amount. The record itself says where that document is kept.

**It has not quietly changed since.** When you correct something, you correct it visibly and with a date, so the correction becomes part of the record instead of replacing it.

Every habit in the rest of this course exists to produce records that pass those three tests. None of it is complicated. The difficulty is entirely in doing it near the time, which is why the next lesson removes the largest obstacle to that: money sitting in one undifferentiated pile.

## Before the next lesson

Write down the last time somebody asked you to show something about your money, and what you actually sent them. If nobody has ever asked, write down who is likeliest to ask you first this year. That person is your real deadline.

lessons.title: Separating Business Money From Personal Money
lessons.content_mdx:
# Separating Business Money From Personal Money

Everything in the last lesson gets cheap or expensive depending on one decision, and you can make it this afternoon.

Joel does motion graphics for two agencies in Iligan. Client payments land in the same account as his rent, the money he sends his mother, his game top-ups and the transfers to the sari-sari store downstairs. In January somebody asks him what he earned from agency work last year. There is no answer in that account. There is only a river.

## Why one account cannot be untangled later

You might think the transactions are all still sitting there, so the information is still there too. It is not, and the reason is simple: a bank line records an amount, a date and a counterparty, and nothing else. It does not record why.

A transfer to your cousin might be a gift, a loan repayment, or paying a subcontractor who helped you on a client job. A card charge might be a subscription you use only for client work, only for yourself, or for both. The bank cannot tell you which. Only you can, and only while you still remember, and that window closes faster than anyone expects.

Separation is not tidiness. It is a way of recording the why at the moment you still know it, using an account as the label.

## What it looks like at freelance scale

You do not need a company. You need a boundary.

**One account or wallet is the business one.** Client money arrives there. Business spending leaves from there. Nothing else touches it.

**You pay yourself on a schedule.** Once or twice a month, one transfer from the business side to your personal side. That transfer is your pay. Rent, groceries, savings and everything else happen on the far side of it, and none of that is this course's business.

Make it one labelled movement rather than a dozen small withdrawals whenever cash runs low. A dozen withdrawals is twelve rows you have to explain and cannot. One transfer per period is one row that explains itself, and it lets you see what you actually paid yourself last quarter, which is a figure worth having.

What kind of account, at which institution, and what you need to open it: that is not a question this course can answer, because requirements, balances and charges differ by provider and change. Ask the institution directly what a self-employed person opens and what to bring. A second ordinary account used only for business is a legitimate starting point and far better than nothing.

## The messy edges, handled honestly

**The subscription that renews on your personal card.** It happens. Do not pretend it did not. Record the charge in your business records with a note saying it was paid personally, keep the document, then go and change the card. The rule is record it, mark it, stop doing it.

**Cash from a client.** It goes into the business account, not into your pocket. Yes, that is an extra trip. It is also the only way that payment ever becomes evidence.

**A client who keeps paying into your personal account** because that is where they have always sent it. Send the new details in writing, and until the change takes effect, move each payment across on the day it lands with a note naming the invoice it settles.

## If you are already mixed

Do not retro-fit. Reconstructing eight months of tangled transactions is the panic week from the last lesson with extra steps.

Pick a date instead. The first of next month will do. From that date the boundary exists and every transaction lands on the correct side of it. For what came before, do one bounded job: pull out only the client payments, list them with their dates and amounts, and label that list as reconstructed along with the date you built it. Then leave the rest alone.

A clean line with a documented mess behind it is defensible. A mess everywhere is not.

## One honest limit

Separating your money is a bookkeeping decision. It is not a legal shield. If you are self-employed rather than a company, the money in the business account is still your own money and your obligations are still yours personally. Nobody is protected by a second account. What the second account buys you is the ability to answer questions.

Budgeting the personal side, on income that arrives unevenly, is the Basic Finance course's subject and it is a genuinely different skill. This course starts at the moment money becomes business money, and stops again at the moment you pay yourself.

## Before the next lesson

Choose the date your boundary starts, and write it down where you will see it. Then write one sentence saying how you will pay yourself: how often, and from which side to which side.

lessons.title: What Makes a Record Trustworthy
lessons.content_mdx:
# What Makes a Record Trustworthy

Nobody who looks at your books is grading your handwriting. They are running four tests, usually without announcing them. Learn the tests and you can run them on yourself before anybody else does.

## Test one: contemporaneous

Written near the time it happened.

Nobody will ask you when you wrote a row. They find out by asking about one. A row written the same week comes with something attached to it: which call, which file, which of the two similar jobs. A row written four months late answers with a pause, and the pause is the finding.

A date you remembered in March is a guess wearing a date's clothes. A description you wrote in March is worse, because by then you have merged two similar jobs into a single memory and you genuinely no longer know which client the ₱3,500 was for.

The practical version of this test is a weekly habit rather than a daily one. Sunday night, ten minutes, everything that moved this week goes in. A week-old memory is still a memory. A four-month-old memory is fiction.

## Test two: sourced

Every row points at a document that exists, and the row says where that document is.

This is the property that turns a spreadsheet from a diary into evidence. Without it, your ledger is a list of things you assert. With it, every line has something behind it that somebody else produced: a statement line, an invoice you issued, a receipt, a written confirmation from the client.

The check is one question, asked about one row somebody picked more or less at random: where is this from. The answer arrives in ten seconds or it does not arrive, and there is no third outcome.

If a row has no document, the row still goes in. You write in the reference column that there is none, and say what you have instead. An admitted gap is a record. A hidden gap gets found by whoever is checking, and once they find it they start doubting the rows that were fine.

## Test three: complete

The small ones are in there too.

There is a strong pull toward recording only the transactions that feel significant. It feels efficient. It destroys the ledger, because a reviewer who spots one missing ₱200 charge has learned that your records are selective, and now has no way of knowing what else was left out. They start doubting the ₱40,000 rows.

Which is why the check runs on the small ones. A large transaction is the one you were always going to record. The cheapest row to leave out is the smallest, so that is the row somebody looks for.

Completeness is also what makes your own totals mean anything. A category total is only useful if everything in that category is actually inside it.

## Test four: stable

You correct with a new dated line, not by quietly overwriting an old one.

You will make mistakes. You will categorise something wrongly, or record a payment at the amount you invoiced when the statement shows less arriving. The fix is not to go back and change the old number so the sheet looks like it was always right. The fix is a new row, dated today, saying what changed and why, with the old row left exactly where it is.

This feels pedantic until the first time somebody asks why a figure differs from one you sent them in June. If you overwrote it, you have no answer. If you corrected it visibly, the answer is sitting right there and takes ten seconds.

## The four things freelancers produce instead

**The screenshot folder.** Hundreds of files called Screenshot_20260114_193302.jpg. The evidence exists and cannot be found, which in practice is the same as not existing.

**The notebook that stops in February.** Started with real energy. Abandoned during a busy week. Now it is worse than nothing, because it implies a complete record and is not one.

**The one-sitting ledger.** Typed up in April from bank history. Every row is real, and no row knows why the money moved. It is a reasonable starting point, but it has to be labelled as reconstructed, with the date you built it, and the rows you were unsure about marked as unsure.

**The rounded figure.** A payment of ₱12,437.50 written down as ₱12,400 because the round number reads nicer. Now your ledger will never agree with your statement, every total inherits the error, and you get to spend an evening hunting a difference you created on purpose.

## Filing, in two sentences

Filing and naming are the spreadsheets course's chapter 1, and the rule there is the one to use: the date first, then the counterparty, then what the document is, one folder per year and one folder per month inside it. What that course does not cover is the part this one needs from it, which is that paper gets photographed the day it reaches you and the photo goes into the same folder under the same name.

Store all of it somewhere you will still have access to after you change phones or hand back a borrowed laptop. That is a decision about your own accounts, and it is worth ten minutes before three years of files depend on the answer.

## How long you have to be able to answer

One more reason not to throw anything out. Records that support a filing have to be kept, and a required period is attached to them. How long that period runs, what form the records have to be in, and when the clock starts are set by rule, and rules move, so this course prints no number for any of it. Ask the BIR, then write the answer into the year's folder with the date you asked and who told you. Until you have that answer, keeping costs you storage and destroying cannot be undone.

## Before the next chapter

Rename the last five payment screenshots on your phone using the date-first rule, and move them into a folder for the month they belong to. That is the entire habit, at a size you can finish tonight.

quiz.prompt: Reyna has been paid into her personal e-wallet for eight months, mixed in with family transfers and load top-ups. One client now asks for a statement of everything they paid her last year. What should she do?

options.text: Export the whole wallet history for the year and send it, noting which lines the client should ignore.
Build the statement from that client's invoices and payments only, marking any line she cannot evidence.
Work out the amounts from her rate and the months she worked, then ask the client to confirm the total looks right.
Tell the client the older records are gone, and offer a statement running from this month onward.

quiz.explanation: The client asked about their own transactions, so the statement is built from the documents that concern them: her invoices and the payments that settled them. Sending the whole wallet history hands over her family's transfers and makes the client do her work for her, and a note telling them what to skip does not fix that. Rate multiplied by months is a guess, and asking the client to confirm a guess makes it their problem rather than evidence. Where she genuinely cannot evidence a payment, the honest move is to mark it as such rather than smooth it over.

quiz.prompt: In April, Ariel types up a ledger covering January to March in one sitting, reading every row off his bank history. Each row is a real transaction. How should he treat the sheet?

options.text: As a labelled reconstruction: note the date he built it, and flag the rows whose purpose he is unsure of.
As unusable, since nothing written months after the fact can be relied on at all.
As finished work, since every row traces to a real bank line, and ask the bank to confirm the doubtful ones.
As a rough draft to retype later, once he has asked each client to confirm what their transfers were for.

quiz.explanation: Reconstruction from statements is honest work and much better than reconstruction from memory, but a bank line records an amount, a date and a counterparty and never why the money moved. The bank cannot tell him either, so asking it confirms nothing he did not already have. Labelling the sheet as reconstructed, with the date he did it, and marking the rows he is unsure about keeps it defensible. Writing it off as unusable throws away real evidence. Waiting until every client answers leaves three months unrecorded, and some of them will never answer.

quiz.prompt: Rico keeps every proof of payment as a phone screenshot. The folder holds hundreds of files named like Screenshot_20260114_193302.jpg. A client queries one payment from last March and he cannot find it. What actually fixes this?

options.text: Keep the screenshots as they are and search the phone gallery by the date the payment was made.
Move every screenshot into one folder called Proofs, so at least nothing is scattered any more.
Rename each file so the date comes first, then the counterparty, then what the document is, and file it in that month's folder.
Ask the client to resend their own proof, since their copy records the same transfer as his.

quiz.explanation: Evidence you cannot find is, for every practical purpose, evidence you do not have. A date-first filename sorts the folder into order by itself and tells you what the file is without opening it, and a folder per month means you are searching a handful of files rather than hundreds. Searching a gallery by date works only when you already know the date, which is the thing in dispute. One big folder is the same problem with a nicer name. Asking the client to supply the proof puts your record in their hands.

quiz.prompt: A design tool Marisol uses only for client work renews every month on her personal card, and switching the card is a chore she keeps postponing. What should she do about her books in the meantime?

options.text: Leave it out of the business records, and note the card change on her list of things to get round to.
Put it on the personal side only, but note the client use in the description so the purpose is not lost.
Start recording it in the business records from the month she moves the card across, and mark the earlier months as personal.
Record the charge with a note that it was paid personally, keep the document, and then change the card.

quiz.explanation: The test for a record is whether it describes what happened. The charge happened and it was for client work, so it goes in, with a note naming which card paid it and the document kept alongside. Leaving it out makes the category total wrong and hides a cost that repeats every month, however good the note on the to-do list is. Filing it as personal because of which card was used records the mechanism instead of the purpose, and a description does not undo a row on the wrong side. Marking the earlier months as personal is the same error written down twice.

quiz.prompt: At a family gathering, an uncle tells Grace that freelancers only have to keep records for a set number of years, and that she can throw out anything older than that. What is the right response?

options.text: Follow it, since a rule about how long to keep papers is not the sort of thing that moves.
Keep everything for now, and confirm the current rule with the BIR or an accountant.
Clear out the oldest year, noting what she destroyed, as a middle position between the two.
Keep only what a client might ask about, and ask her groupmates what they do with the rest.

quiz.explanation: The obligation to keep records is real, and chapter 1 told you a required period is attached to it. What that period is, and what form the records have to be in, are set by rules that change, and an uncle at a party is not a source. The move is to confirm the current rule with the BIR or an accountant and write down the date you checked, so that next year you know how old your answer is. Meanwhile keeping costs you a folder and destroying cannot be undone. A noted middle position is still a guess, and a groupmate is the same uncle with better wifi.

quiz.prompt: A client payment of ₱12,437.50 lands in Ella's business account. She writes ₱12,400 in her ledger because the round figure reads more nicely. What does this habit actually cost her?

options.text: Nothing worth worrying about, since the difference is small and the rounding went in the safe direction.
Only that her recorded income reads slightly low, which is a cautious way to keep her figures.
Every total built on that row is now wrong, and she has made a difference she will have to hunt down at the close.
The client will notice the mismatch when they check their own books against her invoice.

quiz.explanation: Rounding breaks reconciliation, which is the check that makes a ledger trustworthy: the row is meant to match a statement line exactly, and a row that does not match cannot be ticked off. Every category total and every yearly figure inherits the error, and the evening spent chasing the difference is spent on one she created herself. Rounding downward is not conservative, it is just wrong in a chosen direction. Whether the client notices is beside the point, because the person who has to reconcile this is her. Record the figure the statement shows, awkward centavos included.

quiz.prompt: A client insists they already settled an invoice from two months ago. All Nadine has is a Messenger thread where the client wrote sending now. Her business account shows no matching credit. What is her position?

options.text: Strong on both the invoice and the missing credit, so ask the client for their proof of transfer.
Weak, so the practical move is to write the amount off and be more careful with the next client.
Neutral, since with one message on each side it comes down to whoever pushes hardest for longest, so she should note the dispute and move on.
Strong, because the client's own message saying they were sending it confirms that the payment was made.

quiz.explanation: Sending now records an intention, not a transfer, and a message confirming an intention is not a confirmation of payment. What Nadine holds is stronger than she thinks: a numbered invoice she issued, and a business account statement showing no matching credit in that period. That pair is checkable by a stranger, which a chat message is not. So the next step is to ask the client for their proof of transfer with the date, amount and reference, and check it against the same statement. Note what makes this work: had the money been landing in a personal account mixed with everything else, she would have no clean statement to point at.

quiz.prompt: Ferdie is setting up his records as one spreadsheet plus a folder of documents per month. He works from a phone he replaces every couple of years and a laptop borrowed from his sister. What deserves ten minutes of thought before he starts?

options.text: Whether documents are kept as photos or as PDFs, and noting the format on each row so nothing is ambiguous.
Which spreadsheet application to pay for, since the paid ones are the ones that handle books properly.
How many columns the sheet will need, since adding one later would break the formulas he has written by then.
Where the files will live, so he still has access after the phone is replaced and the laptop goes back.

quiz.explanation: The tooling questions are answerable later and cheaply. Access is the one that is expensive to fix afterwards, because records you cannot reach are records you do not have, and a phone gets replaced and a borrowed laptop goes back to its owner. Columns can be added to a sheet whenever you need them, and a formula that breaks tells you it broke. A legible photo and a PDF are both fine as evidence, so noting which one it is buys him nothing. Decide where everything lives and under whose account before three years of files depend on the answer.

lessons.title: Three Documents, Three Different Jobs
lessons.content_mdx:
# Three Documents, Three Different Jobs

Jomar edits video in Mandaue for two small agencies. A third client, a corporation with an actual accounting department, sends him an onboarding form. One line asks what document he can issue for his fees. He does not know what the question is asking, so he attaches a screenshot of a GCash transfer from a different client and submits it. Onboarding stalls there.

The screenshot was the wrong document, and not because Jomar was careless. Freelancers use three words for paperwork as though they were one word. They name three different jobs, and only one of them is the job that form was asking about.

## Three jobs, not three synonyms

**A request to be paid.** Call it a billing statement; the word invoice now belongs to the regulated document below. You write it, you issue it, and it says what you are owed and why. It proves what you claimed. It does not prove that anything was paid.

**An acknowledgement that money changed hands.** A receipt in the ordinary sense of the word: a document saying an amount was received, from whom, on what date, and for what. A bank statement line and a wallet history entry are evidence of the same event, recorded by the channel rather than by you.

**The document a registered seller is required to issue.** This is the regulated one, and unlike the exact rates elsewhere in this course, the two names in play here are stable enough to learn outright. Since the Ease of Paying Taxes Act reformed this area, the working split is between a **Sales Invoice**, which is the document that evidences the sale itself, the billing, and an **Official Receipt**, which evidences that a payment was actually collected. Which one (or both) a given registered freelancer issues, in what sequence, and what has to be printed on it are exactly the kind of specifics that move with each new BIR issuance, so this lesson names the two terms and stops there.

Take the current requirement from the BIR or from an accountant, ask about your own situation rather than about freelancers in general, and write down the date you asked. Knowing the two names lets you ask a precise question instead of a vague one; it does not tell you which one applies to you yet.

## Why this is a commercial question first

Jomar's immediate problem was not a penalty. It was a form he could not fill in, in front of a client who needed an answer before they could set him up as a payee at all. That is the shape of the risk for a freelancer. Not knowing what you can issue costs you the conversation long before it costs you anything else.

Which makes the fix ordinary. Find out what you can issue, say exactly that, and name what you are still checking. Never promise a document you have not confirmed you can produce, because a promise you cannot keep is worse than a gap you named on day one.

Something you could send today:

> I can send a billing statement with my details and the work described, and a written acknowledgement of payment once the transfer lands. I am confirming with the BIR what else applies to me, and I will come back to you on Friday.

## The billing document you can issue today

Careful with the word. Legislation has been moving these terms around, and invoice is one of the words it moved onto the regulated document a registered seller issues. So do not put that word on anything you hand a client until you have confirmed with the BIR what you are entitled to issue and what it has to be called. What follows is the content, not the label. Head it something neutral, Billing Statement or Request for Payment.

What a payable billing document has to carry is the freelancing course's subject and that list has not changed: who is billing, who is billed, a number, a date, what the work was in the words of the agreement, the amount and the terms, and exactly how to pay you with the reference to put on the transfer. What that course does not cover is what turns a pile of them into records, which is the numbering and the copies.

Elsewhere this course still says invoice, because that is the word you and your client will both use out loud and the word your own numbering uses. The care is about the label on a document you hand somebody, and about what you tell a client you are able to issue.

## Numbering that does not collide

Pick one sequence and never break it. The year plus a running count is enough: INV-2026-001, then INV-2026-002. Never reuse a number, never restart in the middle of a year, and never let two clients share one.

If you cancel an invoice, do not recycle its number. Issue a new one, and note on your copy that the old number was cancelled and when. A gap in a sequence is a question you can answer. A repeated number is a question you cannot.

## Keep your own copy of everything you issue

Save the billing document as a file the moment you send it, named with the date and its number, in the month folder you set up in chapter 1. Save the acknowledgement you send when the money arrives, in the same place, named the same way.

Clients change staff. Threads get archived. Apps get uninstalled and phones get stolen. The copy you control is the only one you can count on when somebody asks you in eleven months what you billed them in March, and being the person who can answer that in a day is worth more to a client than any of the paperwork feels while you are doing it.

lessons.title: Proving the Money Came In

# Proving the Money Came In

Bea does inbox and calendar work for three clients from Davao. One pays her by bank transfer, one through a freelancing platform, and one sends cash with a relative who works two jeepney rides away. In March a client asks her to confirm what they paid her across last year. She has the money. She cannot show where any of it came from.

Income evidence is the half of bookkeeping that looks easy until somebody asks. The money arriving is not the record. The record is the thing you can still put in front of a stranger a year later.

## What each channel hands you, and for how long

Each channel records the event in its own way, so you are looking for a different object in each one.

- From a bank, the statement line: a date, an amount, and whatever it shows about the sender.
- From a wallet, the transaction entry and whatever reference sits on it.
- From a platform, its own record that a payment was released to you.
- From a remittance, the advice or the slip and the reference on it.
- From a client, a message saying "sent na po", which is a claim rather than evidence.

Do not assume any of these will still be reachable when you need it. How far back a history goes, whether it can be exported, and in what form all differ by provider and change without anyone telling you. So find out what your own accounts give you this week, while nothing is urgent.

Then take the object out at the time and keep it: the statement each month, a screenshot with the date and reference visible, the platform's own record of the release. Saving at the time costs you a minute. Retrieving in a year costs you an email chain, and sometimes costs you the record entirely.

## Matching a payment to the invoice it settles

Proof that money arrived is only half the job. The other half is knowing which invoice it settled, because that is what turns a pile of deposits into a set of answers.

Give every row a **document reference**: a short code naming the file that holds the evidence. The row says what happened, the reference says where the proof lives, and chapter 3 builds the sheet around that column. Bea's reference for a March transfer might read `2026-03-14-bank-stmt-p2`, which is enough to find the file in the folder from chapter 1 without opening four others first.

Four awkward cases fill a freelancer's year.

**One payment covering two invoices.** Say Bea invoiced ₱8,000 and ₱4,500 in the same month, and a single transfer of ₱12,500 arrives. Those figures are invented so the shape is visible; yours will be different. Record two rows, one against each invoice, both pointing at the same document reference, with a note that they arrived together. A single row for ₱12,500 against nothing is a row that will defeat you in November.

**A partial payment.** Record what actually arrived, against the invoice it belongs to, and leave that invoice showing a balance still open. Do not edit the invoice down to match the money that came. The gap is the useful information.

**An advance paid before the work.** The money is in your account and the job has not started. Record it on the day it arrived, mark on the row that it is an advance against a named job, and settle it against the invoice when you issue one.

**A payment under a name you do not recognise.** A spouse, a business manager, a company's disbursement account, a relative sending on somebody's behalf. Do not leave it sitting as a mystery deposit, and do not quietly guess. Ask the client in writing to confirm that the payment came from them and what it covers, then save that reply beside the bank line. Two objects, one row.

## Cash, where there is no line to point at

Cash leaves no trail unless you make one. When somebody hands you money, write an acknowledgement on the spot: the date, the amount in words and in figures, what it is for, which invoice it settles, your name, the payer's name, and both signatures. Photograph it before either of you walks away.

That photo is the only evidence that will ever exist for that transaction. It cannot be reconstructed later, and remembering it clearly is not the same as being able to show it.

## What this buys you

Bea's client in March was not accusing her of anything. They were closing their own books and needed a number they could rely on. A freelancer who can answer that in a day, with references attached, is a freelancer who gets asked back.

The habit is three moves and it fits in a week. Money lands. You save the object. You write the row, and the row names the object.

lessons.title: Proving an Expense Was Business
lessons.content_mdx:
# Proving an Expense Was Business

Say this plainly before anything else. This lesson is about evidence, not about deductions. Writing a cost into your books does not make it deductible, and nothing here tells you what the BIR will allow. Whether a given expense reduces what you owe is a question for the rules current at the time, or for an accountant looking at your actual situation.

What the lesson does give you is the ability to answer one question about any peso you spent. What business purpose did this serve, and can you say it out loud to a stranger without flinching.

## The three piles

Rowena writes product copy for e-commerce brands from her family's house in Antipolo. Take one month of her spending and sort it.

**Clean.** A stock image subscription she uses only for client decks. An external drive bought to hold one client's raw files. The renewal on her own portfolio domain. Each of these exists because the business exists. The purpose is a sentence, and the sentence is boring, which is exactly what you want.

**Mixed.** Her internet, shared with four other people in the house. Electricity. Phone load. Her share of the rent. A laptop she works on and her brother games on. These are real costs of doing the work, and they are also the household's costs. Pretending either half is not there is where freelancers get into trouble.

**Personal, and it felt like work.** Dinner with a friend who might refer her someday. A course she bought during a slow week and never opened. Shoes for a client meeting held on Zoom. A feeling of relevance is not a business purpose.

Sorting one real month into those three piles is a single sitting, and it will teach you more about your books than any tool will.

## For mixed costs, write down the basis

Nobody can hand you the right split. Any number printed in a course would be a number invented for a person who is not you. What you can do is choose a basis you are willing to explain, then be consistent about it.

A basis is a rule with a reason attached. Rowena works in one of the five rooms in the house and uses it for nothing else, so she splits rent and electricity by rooms. She already logs her working hours, so she splits the internet bill by hours of use in an ordinary week. The laptop is genuinely shared, and she is not willing to claim all of it.

Three moves turn that from a guess into a record.

1. Write the basis down in one sentence, on a reference tab or in a note in the year's folder.
2. Write the date you chose it and what you based it on.
3. Apply the same basis every month, and when the situation changes, revisit it with a new dated line rather than a silent edit.

A client's finance team, a reviewer or an accountant is not looking for a perfect number. They are looking at whether you had a method, whether you can explain it, and whether February and September were treated the same way. An inconsistent split is a far bigger problem than a conservative one.

Say it once more, because this is the lesson where the temptation lives. A split you have documented is evidence of how you arrived at a figure. It is not a ruling that the figure is allowed. That ruling comes from the BIR or from an accountant, and you go and ask.

## When the supplier gives you nothing

The sari-sari store that sold you bond paper. The tricycle and then the jeepney to a client's office in Ortigas, paid in cash to both. The neighbour who repaired your chair. Sometimes there is no document at all.

Do not skip the row, and do not invent a document. Record it the same day with everything you do have: the date, the amount, who you paid, what it was for, and how you paid it. If there is a transfer or a wallet entry behind it, that is your reference. If it was cash, write your own dated note and file it with the month's papers.

An expense with a thin record and an honest note is defensible. An expense with no record at all, remembered in April, is not.

## The three things that travel together

For every business cost, at the time it happens:

- **The document**, saved and named the way chapter 1 set out
- **The row**, carrying the document reference, so the two can find each other
- **The purpose**, in a few plain words, written while you still know why

"Stock image subscription, March, used on the Salcedo bakery deck and two client carousels" is a purpose. "Software" is not, and by October you will not be able to tell those two spends apart.

Chapter 3 turns these rows into a working sheet. This chapter's job was to make sure that every row you write there will have something real standing behind it.

quiz.prompt: Jomar's new corporate client sends an onboarding form. One line asks what document he can issue for his fees, and he has never been asked this before. What should he put in that box?

options.text: That he will issue an official receipt, then ask around online for what one has to contain and copy a template that matches.
A screenshot of a transfer from an earlier client, marked with the date, as evidence he has been paid before.
A note saying what he can issue today, what he is still confirming with the BIR, and when he will confirm the rest.
A request that the client name the document they need, and a note promising to provide whatever they write on the form.

quiz.explanation: What a registered seller is required to issue, what it is called, and what a buyer needs on their side have been changed by legislation and keep moving, so a template copied off the internet risks issuing the wrong thing under a name that no longer applies. Promising whatever the client names is the same guess with the client's wording on it. A transfer screenshot proves money moved, not what he can issue, and a date on it does not change that. Naming what he can do today and what he is still checking keeps the onboarding alive and keeps him honest.

quiz.prompt: Bea sees ₱6,000 land in her account from "M. Ramirez". She has no client by that name, but a dental clinic she invoiced for exactly ₱6,000 has not paid yet. What should she do first?

options.text: Ask the clinic to confirm in writing who sent the payment and what it settles, then save the reply beside the bank line.
Record it as income from the clinic, since the amount matches the open invoice and no other client owes her exactly that figure.
Leave it out of the ledger until somebody asks about it, so that her books never carry a row whose source she cannot explain.
Record it under an unknown heading and note it for the year end, when she reconciles the whole year in one sitting.

quiz.explanation: A matching amount is a strong hint and not evidence. Clinics pay through an owner's personal account, a spouse, or a disbursement officer, and they also sometimes pay the wrong freelancer. One message costs nothing and produces a second document that sits beside the bank line for good. Waiting for somebody to ask leaves a gap between the statement and the ledger that she will have to explain anyway, and a year-end pile of unknowns is the reconstruction problem this course exists to prevent, whether or not each one carries a note.

quiz.prompt: Nina issued INV-2026-011 for ₱8,000 and INV-2026-012 for ₱4,500 to the same client. A single transfer of ₱10,000 arrives with no reference on it at all. How should she record it?

options.text: One row for the full ₱10,000 against the larger invoice, with a note that the client still owes the difference.
One row for ₱10,000 with no invoice named, since the client never said which of the two jobs the money was for.
Two rows of ₱5,000, one against each invoice, so both are left showing the same amount outstanding.
Ask the client how the ₱10,000 splits across the two invoices, then write one row per invoice and save the reply as the evidence for both.

quiz.explanation: Only the client knows what they intended, and the split decides which invoice you chase next month. Halving it is an invented figure that will not match their records. Putting all of it against the larger invoice leaves ₱2,000 sitting against nothing, and a note about the difference does not say which invoice it belongs to. A row with no invoice named is the row that defeats you in November. One question now produces both the arithmetic and the document that supports it.

quiz.prompt: A client sends Ellen ₱5,000 to start on a job that has not begun, and she has not issued an invoice yet. What belongs in her records today?

options.text: Nothing yet. She waits until the job is finished and the invoice is issued, then records the whole agreed fee on that later date.
A row dated the day the money arrived, marked as an advance against the named job.
A row recording it as a loan from the client, since none of it has been earned and no work has been delivered.
A row for the full agreed fee now, noting that the balance will follow once she delivers the work.

quiz.explanation: Money that arrived on a date is recorded on that date, whatever it is for. Waiting for the invoice puts her ledger out of step with the bank statement, which is the mismatch that makes a monthly reconciliation painful. Recording the full fee records money she does not have, and a note saying the rest is coming does not make the row true today. Calling it a loan describes an arrangement neither of them agreed to. An advance is money received with a job named against it, and that mark is what lets her settle it cleanly later.

quiz.prompt: Rowena works from a house in Antipolo where the internet is shared with four other people. She wants the business share of the bill in her books. What is the defensible way to do it?

options.text: Put the whole bill in, on the ground that without a connection she could not do a single hour of client work from that house.
Leave the internet out of the books completely, since it is a household bill and any split she chose would be arguable.
Estimate a different share each month depending on how heavy the client work felt, noting that month's reasoning on the row.
Choose a basis she can explain, note the basis and the date, and apply that same basis every month until it stops fitting.

quiz.explanation: A reviewer is testing method and consistency, not precision. A written basis with a date behind it survives being questioned even if somebody would have chosen differently. A share that moves with how the month felt is an opinion recorded monthly, and writing the reasoning down each time documents the inconsistency rather than curing it. The whole bill ignores four other people on the same line. Leaving it out entirely means her books understate the real cost of the work, which distorts every judgement she makes about pricing.

quiz.prompt: Marco bought a laptop he uses for client editing and his household uses for streaming. He asks whether he can deduct it. What should he do?

options.text: Record the cost with its document and a note on how the laptop is used, then ask the BIR or an accountant.
Keep it out of his books until an accountant has confirmed in writing that a laptop shared with a household can be deducted at all.
Record the full purchase price as a business expense, since he bought the machine for the client work and the streaming came later.
Use the split another freelancer posted online for shared laptops, noting that it is a common arrangement for this kind of machine.

quiz.explanation: Your books record what you spent and why. They do not decide what is allowed, and that decision belongs to the rules current at the time or to a professional looking at your situation. Waiting for permission before recording anything leaves a hole in the ledger and loses the document while he waits. Claiming the whole machine ignores household use he already knows about. A number somebody posted online is a stranger's guess about a different set of facts, and noting that it is common does not put any reasoning of his own behind it.

quiz.prompt: Rowena pays cash for a tricycle and then a jeepney to reach a client's office in Ortigas, and is given nothing for either fare. Her ledger rows are supposed to name their evidence. What now?

options.text: Leave the fares out and note the trip in her diary, since a row with no document weakens every row that has one.
Add them at month end from memory, in one batch with the rest of the month's small cash travel, and mark the whole total as estimated.
Write her own dated note the same day with the amounts, the route and the purpose, file it in that month's folder, and reference it.
Round them into the next expense that does have a document, so the money is noted somewhere and the row still names a real file.

quiz.explanation: Some suppliers will never give you a document, and the answer is to make one rather than to pretend the cost did not happen. A note written the same day and filed where the row can point at it is thin evidence, but it is contemporaneous and honest, which is what survives being questioned. A diary the ledger cannot reach is not evidence for a row that does not exist. Reconstructing at month end produces guesses, and marking them estimated only records that they are guesses. Folding them into another expense corrupts a row that was true before, and now neither row matches its document.

quiz.prompt: Liza is not registered with the BIR. A small business client pays her and asks for a receipt for their records. What should she send?

options.text: A note explaining that a receipt is not needed for an amount this small, along with a screenshot of the transfer for their files.
A billing statement and a written acknowledgement of the payment, a note on what she cannot yet issue, and a date to confirm the rest.
An official receipt filled in from a template she found online, so the client's records are complete and nobody has to wait around for it.
A message agreeing to send the right document next week, once she has asked somebody what the right document is.

quiz.explanation: She can always bill a client in writing and acknowledge a payment, and both are useful to the client. What she cannot do is produce a regulated document she is not in a position to issue, and a template filled in from the internet is exactly that. She should also watch what she calls the thing she sends, because legislation has moved the regulated document's name and the word she reaches for may now belong to it. Telling a business client that no document is needed decides something on their behalf that is not hers to decide. Agreeing to send one next week buys a week and then breaks a promise.

lessons.title: The Columns That Do the Work
lessons.content_mdx:
# The Columns That Do the Work

Teddy does admin support for two clients from Tarlac. His sheet has three columns: date, client, amount. It took him four minutes to set up and it has never once answered a question. When a client asked which invoices a single transfer covered, he could not say. When he wanted to know whether the smaller retainer was worth the hours, the sheet had nothing in it about what serving that client cost him. The sheet is not wrong. It is just too thin to be useful.

Every column in a ledger exists to answer a question somebody will ask you later. That is the whole test. If you cannot name the question a column answers, delete it. If you can name a question your sheet cannot answer, add the column now, while the answers are still easy to find.

## Two tabs and a reference tab

One tab for money in. One tab for money out. A third tab that is not a ledger at all: your category list, written once and left alone, so that six months of rows use the same words for the same thing.

Keep the two ledgers separate. A single tab holding both, with income positive and expenses negative, looks clever in January and is hard to read by June.

## The columns, and the question each one answers

**Date.** When did this happen. Use the date the money actually moved. If the invoice belongs to a different month, that goes in the notes.

**Client or supplier.** Who was on the other side. Write the name the same way every time, or your totals for one client will split across two spellings.

**Description.** What was this, in plain words a stranger could read. "October retainer, social media" beats "work".

**Document reference.** Where is the proof. This is the column that connects the ledger to the documents chapter 2 had you keep, filed and named the way chapter 1 set out. Write the filename, or the folder and the date. This is the column a client's question lands on, and it decides whether answering takes you a minute or a week.

**Category.** What kind of money is this. Chosen from the reference tab, never invented at the keyboard.

**Account or wallet.** Which account did the money move through. This is the column that lets you tick your ledger against a statement at the end of the month, and without it you will spend the close guessing.

**Gross.** What you earned, or what the supplier charged, before anything was taken off.

**Deductions.** What was taken off on the way. The next lesson is entirely about this column.

**Net.** What actually landed in your account, or what actually left it.

**Currency, peso amount, rate used, rate source.** If a client pays in another currency, the ledger still has to end in pesos. Record which currency, the peso figure, the rate you applied, and where that rate came from. Four small columns you will thank yourself for later.

**Notes.** The one sentence you will not remember. "Paid under her husband's name." "Advance against November."

That is a dozen columns and change, and it looks like a lot until you have filled twenty rows, at which point it takes about as long as the three-column version and answers questions the three-column version cannot.

## Table structure is a separate craft

How a table should be built, meaning one row per thing that happened, dates stored as dates, amounts stored as plain numbers, and no totals sitting inside the data, is taught properly in the spreadsheets course. Learn it there. What this course asks of you is narrower: every transaction gets its own row, and every row names its evidence.

## When a spreadsheet stops being enough

A spreadsheet is the right tool at freelance scale, and it stays right for longer than people expect. You have outgrown it when more than one person needs to write in it at the same time, when you are carrying stock, when you are paying other people regularly, or when whoever files for you wants your records inside a system they already run.

Accounting software exists. Choosing one is a decision to make with the person who files for you, not from a course and not from an advertisement. This course names none of them and quotes no prices.

## Do this now

Open a new sheet. Make the two tabs and the reference tab. Put in last week's transactions, all of them, including the small ones. Then look down the document reference column and see how many rows you can actually fill. The empty ones are your homework for the rest of the week.

lessons.title: Recording What Actually Landed
lessons.content_mdx:
# Recording What Actually Landed

Mika edits video from Cagayan de Oro. She invoiced an overseas client and the amount that reached her bank was noticeably smaller than the amount on her invoice. She did the easy thing: she wrote down the figure that landed and moved on.

Six months later that client queried the invoice. Mika's sheet said one number, the invoice said another, and she had nothing in between to explain the gap. The money was fine. Her ability to explain it was not.

## The rule

Record what you earned. Record each deduction on its own named line. Record what landed. The three have to reconcile, and you have to be able to say where each figure came from.

A gap between an invoice and a deposit is never mysterious. It is some combination of a platform's service fee, a payment processor's charge, a currency conversion, a client withholding part of the fee, and a bank charge on the way in. Each of those is a real event and each deserves a line with its own name. "Fees" as one blob is where defensibility goes to die.

## One worked example, with invented figures

Every number below is made up so that you can watch the arithmetic. Replace all of them with your own.

Say Mika invoiced USD 500, an invented figure. Say the platform took a service fee of USD 45, invented too and not a rate you should assume applies to you. Say the remaining USD 455 converted at an invented rate of 50 pesos to the dollar, a round number picked so the arithmetic stays readable. Say her bank charged 200 pesos to receive the transfer, also invented.

Her income row reads:

- Gross: USD 500, which at the rate used is 25,000 pesos
- Deduction, platform service fee: USD 45, which is 2,250 pesos
- Deduction, receiving bank charge: 200 pesos
- Net: 22,550 pesos

Check it both ways. 25,000 less 2,250 less 200 is 22,550. And 455 dollars at 50 is 22,750, less the 200 peso bank charge, is 22,550. The two roads meet, which is the point of writing it out.

Convert once, at one recorded rate, and let the peso figures carry the rounding. Converting each line at a slightly different rate is how a sheet ends up out by a few pesos with nobody able to say where.

## Pick your rate source and write it down

You need two decisions, made once: which source you take an exchange rate from, and which date you use. Write both on your reference tab with the date you decided, then apply them to every foreign payment after that.

This course names no source and no rate. Pick one you can point at, and record on the row where the figure came from.

Never work backwards. Dividing the pesos that landed by the dollars you invoiced produces a number that looks like a rate and is really the rate plus every fee, blended together and unnameable. Once that number is in your sheet, no deduction can be checked, because they have all disappeared inside it.

## The client who withholds

Some local clients pay part of your fee to the government on your behalf rather than to you, and give you a certificate saying they did. Whether a particular client is required to do that, at what amount, and what it means for you at filing time are not things to take from another freelancer or a group chat. Ask the client what they are doing, and confirm the treatment with the BIR or an accountant.

The bookkeeping is the same either way. Record the gross. Record the withheld amount on its own named line. Mark the certificate as outstanding, and chase it while the client still remembers the payment. A deduction you cannot evidence is money you risk paying twice, and that certificate lives in somebody else's inbox, which means it will not arrive unless you ask.

## Four sanity checks

- **A net larger than a gross.** That cannot happen. Something carries the wrong sign, or the gross was typed short.
- **A deduction with no name.** Find out what it was before you close the month.
- **A category total that jumped.** Either something is miscategorised or something real changed, and you should know which.
- **A month with no expenses at all.** You had expenses. They are not in the sheet yet.

## What you can do now

Take the last payment that arrived smaller than you invoiced. Write the gross, each deduction by name, and the net. If the three do not reconcile, you have just found the thing this lesson exists for, and you found it while the evidence is still retrievable.

lessons.title: The Monthly Close
lessons.content_mdx:
# The Monthly Close

Cecile manages inboxes for three clients from Naga. On the first Saturday of every month she makes coffee, opens one folder and one sheet, and spends about an hour closing the month before. Then she does not think about bookkeeping again until the following Saturday's ten minutes.

That hour is what turns a spreadsheet into books. A ledger nobody ever checks against a statement is a list of things you believed at the time.

## The sequence

1. **Pull the statements.** Every account and every wallet the business used that month. Save the files into the month's folder now, not later.
2. **Tick every statement line against a ledger row.** Line by line. This is the boring part, and it is the part that finds things.
3. **Investigate whatever sits on one side only.** A statement line with no row is a payment you forgot, or a subscription you did not know was still running. A row with no statement line is the wrong account in the account column, or a payment that never actually arrived.
4. **Chase the missing documents.** The receipt, the certificate, the platform statement. Ask now, while the person on the other end still remembers the transaction.
5. **File everything.** One folder per year, one per month, named the way chapter 1 had you name them.
6. **Run the totals.** Income, expenses, by category, by client.
7. **Stop touching the month.**

Step seven is a real step. A month you keep quietly editing is a month with no fixed version, and every number you have ever quoted from it is now questionable.

## Correcting a month you already closed

You will need to. A supplier sends an invoice late, or you find something filed under the wrong category.

Do not reopen the month and silently retype a figure. Add a new line, dated the day you are making the correction, saying plainly what it corrects and why. Anyone reading the sheet afterwards, including you, can then see both the original and the fix. The closed total stays visible, which is the entire reason for closing it.

A record earns trust because you can see what changed in it. Overwriting destroys exactly that.

## What the totals are for

Once the numbers are true, read them for ten minutes:

- Which client paid best for the hours you gave them. The retainer that feels small can turn out to be the profitable one.
- Which subscriptions are still running. Look for the one you forgot.
- What a slow month looks like from the inside, early enough to do something about it instead of afterwards.

This is the part freelancers skip, and it is the only part that pays you back the same week.

## Download the statement while you are already in the folder

Chapter 2 made the case for saving evidence at the time rather than trusting it will still be reachable. A statement is the same object. Pull it during the close, not in the week somebody asks for it. Half a minute a month, and it is the difference between having records and having had them.

## When you are months behind

Arnel had not touched his books since April and it was August. The instinct is to sit down and rebuild the four months from memory and message threads. Do not.

Work backwards from the newest statement instead. Statements are the one source that is complete, dated, and not written by you. Take the newest month first, then the one before it. Where you cannot find a document, write "no document found" in the reference column and leave it visible. A gap left visible is still part of the record. A confident row you invented is not, and it will fail the first time somebody tests it.

## The ten minutes that make the hour possible

Same day each week. Add the week's rows. Save the documents into the folder. Name the ones you are still waiting on.

Do that, and the monthly hour is a check. Skip it, and the monthly hour becomes a reconstruction, which is the experience that teaches people bookkeeping is horrible.

Three closes from now you have a quarter you could hand to anybody who asks for it. Twelve from now you have a year.

quiz.prompt: Mika invoiced an overseas client USD 500. The platform took a service fee, the payout converted to pesos, and her bank charged for the incoming transfer, so a smaller peso figure reached her account. How should the income row carry it?

options.text: Record the gross she invoiced, then each deduction on its own named line, and the net that landed
Record the peso amount that landed as the sale, since that is the figure her bank can confirm
Record the gross in pesos and describe the fee and the bank charge in the notes column
Record the payout left after the platform fee, and treat the bank charge as an expense

quiz.explanation: Gross, each named deduction, then net. The three reconcile, and every line can be pointed at a document. Recording only what landed loses the invoice the payment settles, whatever the bank can confirm about the figure. Pushing the fees into notes means they cannot be totalled or checked. Netting the platform fee off the gross hides one deduction while naming the other.

quiz.prompt: Rowena's local client paid her fee less an amount they say they are remitting to the government on her behalf. The certificate evidencing it has not arrived. What goes in her ledger this month?

options.text: The net she received, with a note to add the rest once the certificate arrives
Nothing yet, because the row cannot be finished until the certificate is actually in her hands
The gross, the withheld amount on its own line, and the certificate flagged as outstanding
The gross, with the withheld amount noted as a business expense for that month

quiz.explanation: The event happened this month, so it is recorded this month: gross, the withheld amount as its own named deduction, and a visible flag that the evidence is still owed to her. Waiting for the document leaves a hole in the month. Recording only the net erases the withholding, and a note to fix it later is not a line anyone can total. Calling it an expense is a treatment question for the BIR or an accountant, not something to settle in a ledger.

quiz.prompt: Checking her sheet, Divine finds an income row where the net is larger than the gross. Both figures are in pesos and the row names one invoice. What does that tell her?

options.text: The gross was entered after the platform fee had already come off, so that fee is counted nowhere
The amount that landed was typed into the gross column too, so both columns hold the same figure
The client's withheld amount was written as a separate expense row instead of on this row
A deduction carries a positive sign, so the sheet added it on rather than taking it off

quiz.explanation: Net is gross less deductions, so a net above a gross is arithmetic that cannot happen, and only one of these four produces it: a deduction carrying the wrong sign gets added rather than subtracted. The other three are real faults worth fixing, and none of them lifts a net above a gross. A gross entered short still sits above the money that actually landed. The same figure in both columns makes them equal, not unequal. A withholding recorded on the wrong row leaves this row's net below its gross and the deduction invisible.

quiz.prompt: Kim invoices in dollars. She divides the pesos that landed by the dollars she invoiced, writes the result in her rate column, and moves on. What has she actually done?

options.text: Nothing wrong, so long as she uses the same method every month and notes it on her reference tab
Blended every fee into the rate, so no deduction on that row can be named or checked
Used the payout date when the invoice date is the convention she ought to follow
Recorded a rate with no source, which she can fix by noting the news rate that day

quiz.explanation: Working backwards from the peso figure produces a number that looks like a rate and is really the rate plus every fee, mixed together and impossible to separate. Consistency does not rescue it, and noting the method on a tab only records that she does it every time. Which date to use is a convention she chooses and writes down, not a fixed right answer. And quoting a rate after the fact does not put the fees back on their own lines.

quiz.prompt: During her monthly close, Cecile ticks her e-wallet statement against her ledger and finds a statement line with no matching row. What does she do?

options.text: Add a row for the amount now and label it unidentified until she can trace it
Leave it alone, since the statement is the real record and her sheet only summarises
Adjust her closing total so the sheet agrees with the statement, and note the difference
Trace it to a payment or a purchase, then add the row and the document reference behind it

quiz.explanation: A one-sided item is the close doing its job, and the close is when the trail is still warm. Trace it, then record it with its evidence. An unidentified row is a placeholder she will never come back to. Treating the statement as the record gives up on categories and documents. Adjusting a total to force agreement makes the sheet balance and stop meaning anything, and a note beside the adjustment still does not say what the money was.

quiz.prompt: Two weeks after closing March, a supplier sends Jomar an invoice dated in March that he never recorded. What is the right correction?

options.text: Open March again, insert the row in date order, and recalculate the March totals
Put it in April at its April date, noting that the charge actually arose back in March
Add a dated adjusting line naming what it corrects, leaving the closed total visible
Keep late items on a list he checks at year end, marking each with the month it belongs to

quiz.explanation: A closed month is corrected in the open, with a dated line that says what changed and why, so the original figure and the fix are both readable. Reopening March and retyping the totals destroys the version he already quoted from. Redating it to April misstates when the cost arose, and a note saying so leaves the misstatement sitting in the figures. A parking list at year end is a reconstruction waiting to happen, however carefully each item on it is marked.

quiz.prompt: Teddy's sheet has three columns: date, client, amount. A client asks which invoices one transfer settled, and he cannot say. Which column would have answered that?

options.text: A document reference column, naming the invoice each payment settles
A running balance column, so each payment reads against the total still owed
A category column, separating client income from the other kinds of income
A notes column, holding whatever he happened to remember at the time he typed the row

quiz.explanation: The document reference is the column that ties a row to the evidence behind it, which is exactly what the client is asking about. A running balance shows what is outstanding but not which invoice a payment cleared. A category tells you what kind of income it was. Notes hold what you remembered, and what you remembered is the thing that failed here.

quiz.prompt: Arnel has not touched his books since April and it is now August. Statements exist for every one of those months. What is the sensible way back?

options.text: Start clean from August, noting that the four missing months are unrecoverable
Work backwards through the statements, newest first, marking the rows he cannot document
Rebuild the four months from memory and message threads, then ask clients to confirm the totals
Wait for the year end and hand the whole untouched period to a bookkeeper

quiz.explanation: Statements are complete, dated and not written by him, so they are the spine to rebuild against, newest first while the trail is warmest. Gaps get marked as gaps and stay visible. Abandoning four months throws away recoverable records, and a note calling them unrecoverable does not make them so. Memory produces confident rows that fail the first challenge, and asking a client to confirm a total he invented invites them to agree to a figure neither of them checked. A bookkeeper handed an untouched shoebox costs more and does worse work.
