lessons.title: What Registration Actually Means
lessons.content_mdx:
# What Registration Actually Means

Rates, exact thresholds and due dates move, and what applies to you depends on how you are classified and on what you earn, so this chapter still will not print a peso figure or a date as fact. What it will do, because these do not move the way rates do, is name the actual pieces of the system: the document registration produces, the forms your income tax return will be filed on, and an option worth asking about by name. Knowing those names is what turns a vague question into a precise one when you do sit down with the BIR or an accountant.

## What an employer was absorbing for you

If you have ever been on a payroll, someone else did a quiet pile of work on your behalf. Your employer computed what to withhold, remitted it, filed on a schedule, and handed you a summary at the end of the year. You saw a deduction on a payslip and nothing else.

Earning from your own trade or profession moves that work to you. It arrives as six obligations, and it helps to see them as shapes rather than as a list of figures you are supposed to have memorised.

**Registering.** You exist in the system as someone earning from their own work rather than through an employer. What that involves, and where, is a question for the BIR, but the document it ends with has a name worth knowing: a **Certificate of Registration**, BIR Form 2303, listing the tax types you are registered for. Keep the original somewhere safe and a photo of it in the document folder from chapter 1, because clients and banks sometimes ask to see it before they will deal with you at all.

**Keeping books.** Records of what came in and what went out, kept in a form the rules recognise. Chapters 1 to 3 built exactly this: the boundary, the documents, the ledger, the monthly close.

**Issuing the document a buyer is entitled to when they pay you.** Chapter 2 covered what these documents do. What the required one is currently called, which transactions call for it, and what you must have in place before you can issue it have all been changed by legislation in recent years. Confirm the current requirement rather than repeating what a client or a groupmate told you.

**Filing returns on a schedule.** Your income tax return is filed on one of the forms in the **1701 family**: 1701, 1701A or 1701Q are the names you will see and hear. Which one is yours, and when each one falls due, depends on your classification and how you are taxed, so that is a question you bring to the BIR rather than a form number you guess at. It is the subject of the next lesson, and you are the one who finds out.

**Choosing how you are taxed.** One option worth asking about by its name rather than discovering by accident: many self-employed individuals below a certain income level can elect an **8% tax on gross receipts** instead of the graduated income tax rates that apply by default. It trades away most deductions for a simpler calculation, and whether you qualify, what the current threshold is, and whether it is the better choice for your numbers are all questions for the BIR or an accountant. Knowing the option exists is what lets you ask about it in year one instead of finding out about it from another freelancer in year three.

**Paying what is assessed.** Filing and paying are separate acts. Keep proof of both.

**Your own contributions.** SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG stop being lines an employer deducts from a payslip and become arrangements you join and pay into yourself. Whether each applies to you as a self-employed member, on what schedule, and what the member benefits are is published by SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG themselves, and this course prints none of it. They belong on the calendar you build in the next lesson, beside anything BIR-facing, because a missed contribution is invisible until the month you need the benefit.

Read that order again. The two that feel like admin, the books and the documents, are what make the rest of them possible. You cannot file a figure you cannot produce, and you cannot produce it from memory in a panicked week.

## Why the details differ, and why that is not evasion

Elmer edits podcasts for an agency in Cebu and a client in Australia. Marilou is a VA in Iloilo with four small local clients. Both are self-employed freelancers, and their obligations are not identical, because classification, what you earn, where the client sits and what you have chosen all feed the answer.

That is why a figure passed around a group chat is dangerous even when nobody is lying. It was somebody's real answer, to their situation, on a date nobody recorded. Marilou acting on Elmer's number is not taking a shortcut. She is answering a different question.

## The questions worth bringing to a BIR office or an accountant

Vague questions get vague answers. Bring closed ones about your own situation, and bring something to write on.

- I earn from local clients and from a client abroad. Which returns apply to me, and when does each one fall due?
- Given roughly what I expect to earn this year, which options are open to me, and what does choosing one commit me to?
- What am I required to give a client when they pay me, and what do I need in place before I can give it?
- Which of my contributions do I make myself now, and does that change how I file?
- What records do you need from me, in what form, and how often?
- What do I have to tell you, or the BIR, when something changes: a new client abroad, a bigger year, a move?
- Where can I read this myself in the BIR's own issuances?

Write down the answer, who gave it, and the date you got it. That last habit is what the next lesson is built on.

## Where the authoritative answer lives

In order: the BIR's own current issuances and its own offices. Then a licensed professional who has seen your actual records. Then everything else, including this course, which is orientation only.

A confident answer from someone with no stake in whether you are right is the most expensive kind. The group chat is not a source. It is a useful place to discover that a question exists.

## Do this before the next lesson

Write one list. Every obligation you think applies to you, and next to each, honestly, whether you know that or assume it. The assumed ones go to the BIR or to an accountant. The next lesson turns the confirmed ones into a calendar.

lessons.title: Building Your Deadline Calendar
lessons.content_mdx:
# Building Your Deadline Calendar

You are about to build a deadline calendar without this course naming a single date. That is not a gap in the lesson. A date you did not check is not a deadline, it is a rumour with a number in it, and this lesson is about the checking.

Every date in the calendar you build comes from the BIR or from your accountant, and you write down which.

## Three categories to go and search for

Before the columns, know what shapes of obligation you are hunting, because a blank table with no starting point is how this lesson used to leave you. Every self-employed person's calendar has rows that fall into three named categories, even before you know a single date.

**Registration renewal.** Anything tied to keeping your registration itself current or up to date with the BIR, separate from any single year's income. Search for what this involves for someone registered as you are.

**Periodic filing.** Returns and payments that recur inside the year, monthly or quarterly depending on the tax type. This is where the 1701Q-style quarterly filing from the last lesson lives, alongside anything else that comes around more than once a year.

**Annual filing.** The once-a-year return that settles the full year, the 1701 or 1701A family the last lesson named, plus any yearly registration-related payment. Search for this as its own row, separate from the quarterly ones, because it is easy to assume the quarterly filings add up to the annual one and they do not.

Add a fourth heading of your own for anything BIR-facing that does not fit the three, and a fifth for the SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG contributions from the last lesson, which run on their own schedules outside the BIR entirely. Five headings, and under each one, at least one row you go and confirm.

## One row per obligation, four columns

Open a tab in the same workbook as your ledger. Give it these columns.

**Obligation.** In your own words. What is due, and to whom. The BIR is not the only answer: any contribution you now make yourself, to SSS, PhilHealth or Pag-IBIG, gets its own row here on the same terms as everything else, confirmed with the body that runs it.

**Due date or frequency.** As confirmed. Not as assumed, and not as remembered.

**Source.** Who told you. A BIR issuance, a BIR office, your accountant by name.

**Date checked.** The day you were told.

The last two columns are what let the calendar survive a year. Anybody can write a date down. A row that cannot say where its date came from is the same rumour you started with, sitting in a spreadsheet where it now looks official.

Sheryl designs social graphics for two agencies in General Santos. Her sheet has a fifth column headed "not yet confirmed". Rows sit in it carrying a question and the date she sent it to someone who can answer. Nothing leaves that column without a source and a date. That column is worth more than the rest of the sheet, because it is the honest list of what she does not know, and it is the thing she brings to an accountant.

## Then put it in a calendar, early

The spreadsheet is the record. The calendar is what actually reminds you. Copy each confirmed obligation into whatever calendar you already look at, and set the reminder well ahead of the date rather than on it.

Lead time is the point, because the due date is rarely the thing that fails. What fails is everything upstream of it:

- a client who owes you a certificate for tax they withheld and has not sent it
- a document you cannot find because it was never filed into the month folder
- an office that is closed, or a queue longer than your afternoon
- a payment channel that is down on the day
- a laptop that dies in the one week you needed it

A reminder that arrives on the due date is telling you about a problem you no longer have time to solve.

## When you already know you will miss one

Hiding is the expensive move. The sequence that works:

1. Find out from an authoritative source what actually happens when this particular one is late. Not what a group says happens. The consequence is a fact about the rules, and it is knowable.
2. Ask what the shortest route back to compliant looks like for your situation.
3. Act at the first opportunity rather than waiting for the next deadline to come round.
4. Write down what you were told, by whom, and when, in the same sheet.

A missed deadline is a problem with a size. Not knowing the size is what turns it into dread, and dread is what makes people leave it another quarter.

## Keep the proof the way you keep income evidence

Chapter 2 had you save proof that money came in. Save proof that money went out to an obligation with the same care: the filing confirmation, the payment confirmation, the reference number. Into the month folder from chapter 1, named the way everything else there is named.

Then put that reference into the document reference column of the ledger row for the payment. A payment you made with no retrievable proof is a payment you can end up making twice.

## The commercial dates belong on the same view

Obligations are not the only dated things in a freelance year. Keeping them on a separate calendar from the commercial ones is how you end up owing money in a week you forgot to invoice.

Put these on the same view:

- the day each retainer invoice goes out
- the date each client runs their payments, if they have a fixed one
- when your own subscriptions renew, so a tool you stopped using does not quietly bill you for another year
- your monthly close day from chapter 3

Seen together, they tell you something a list of due dates cannot. Which weeks are heavy, and which invoice needs to go out early because something falls due soon after it.

## The yearly recheck

Book one appointment with yourself, once a year, in the calendar you just built. The job is to walk down the sheet, ask whether each row is still true, and update the source and date checked columns.

Rules change. So do you: a new client abroad, a bigger year, a different arrangement. A calendar built once and never revisited gets quietly more wrong every year, while looking exactly as confident as it did on the day you made it.

lessons.title: When to Hand It to an Accountant
lessons.content_mdx:
# When to Hand It to an Accountant

The last judgment call in this course is when to stop doing this yourself. It is not a failure point. It is a decision with a cost on both sides, and having read this far you can now make it well.

## The signals

Any one of these is a reason to talk to a professional. Two together is a reason to do it this month.

- Money arriving from several countries, or in several currencies.
- You have taken someone on: an employee, or a subcontractor you use regularly.
- A client is asking for a document you are not sure you can issue, and onboarding is stalled on it.
- A letter or a notice arrived that you do not fully understand.
- Several months of records untouched, getting heavier every month you leave them.
- The plain arithmetic one. The hours you spend on this are worth more spent on client work. If an evening a week goes to admin, price that evening at your own rate and look at the number.

Notice what is not on that list: the size of your income. Small and complicated needs help. Large and simple sometimes does not.

## A bookkeeper and an accountant are not the same hire

A bookkeeper works with the records. Keeping the ledger current, matching documents to rows, closing the month, keeping the file in a state somebody else could pick up. That work is regular, and it is the work this course taught you to do.

An accountant works on top of records that already exist. What your situation requires, what applies to you, what to file, what to do about the letter. That work is occasional, and it costs more per hour.

Freelancers often need the second sometimes and the first more often. Hiring an accountant to sort out a shoebox is paying senior rates for junior work, and both of you will resent it.

## What you hand over is what you already built

Aldrin ships web work from Dumaguete. He put off getting help for two years because he assumed the first meeting would be humiliating. What he eventually walked in with was a ledger with one row per transaction, a folder per month holding the documents those rows point at, one account that had only ever held client money, and a written page of the things he was not sure about.

The meeting ran under an hour and the advice was specific, because there was something to be specific about.

Arriving organised changes both the price and the quality of what you get. The price, because nobody is billing you to reconstruct your year first. The quality, because an adviser looking at real records can answer your situation, while an adviser looking at estimates can only answer in general.

The written page of what you are unsure about is the part people skip and the part that earns the most. It is the same list as the not yet confirmed column from the last lesson.

## Choosing someone

Ask five questions before you engage anybody.

- What do you need from me each month, and in what form?
- How do you want to receive it?
- What is not included in what you do for me?
- How do you charge, and for what scope?
- Who exactly will be doing the work?

Then check that the person is who they say they are, through whatever verification the relevant professional body itself offers, rather than through a screenshot of a certificate in a chat. If any of those five answers comes back vague, that vagueness is the thing you will be arguing about in eight months.

Ask one more thing during the first engagement: show me where in the rules this comes from. A good adviser is not annoyed by that question.

## What stays yours whoever you hire

Two things do not transfer.

You are the one who signs. Whatever is filed under your name is yours, and "my bookkeeper did it" is not a position you want to be standing in.

And you are the one who has to know what your own numbers mean. Not the rules, not the rates. Your numbers: what you earned, what it cost you to earn it, which client is worth the hours, what is still sitting unpaid. Delegating the filing is sensible. Delegating the knowing is how a freelancer ends up learning about their own business from a stranger.

That is also the honest answer about AI here. Whatever helps you draft or organise, you remain the one who signs, and a fluent answer about a rule is not a source.

## The last word

What this course has given you is smaller than advice and more useful: records you can stand behind, the names of the documents and forms you will actually meet, and therefore professional advice that is cheap, fast, and actually about you.

quiz.prompt: Marilou reads in a freelancer Facebook group that a return is due on a particular day next month. The person who posted it sounds certain and several people have thanked them. Marilou is registered and it may well apply to her. What should she do with that date?

options.text: Put it in her calendar exactly as posted, since several people in the group have already confirmed the same date.
Ignore it completely, because nothing posted in a group chat about tax is ever worth acting on.
Treat it as a question, confirm it with the BIR or her accountant, and record the source and the date.
Wait until nearer the date and then ask the group again, to see whether the answer has changed by then.

quiz.explanation: A group chat is a good place to discover that a question exists and a bad place to get its answer: the poster was describing their own situation, on a date nobody recorded, under rules that move. Thanks from other members confirm that the post was popular, not that it was right. Ignoring it entirely wastes the useful half, which is the prompt to go and check. Asking the group again later re-runs the same unreliable process closer to the deadline. Take it to the BIR or your accountant, then write the answer down with who gave it and when, so next year you can tell whether the row has gone stale.

quiz.prompt: Marisol's ledger has not been closed since April, her documents are unfiled, and no row names the evidence behind it. She wants one person to put that right and then keep it right every month. Who should she be looking for, and why?

options.text: A bookkeeper, because keeping the ledger current and matching documents to rows is regular work at the lower rate.
An accountant, because records left in this state need a licensed professional before anyone else is asked to touch them.
An accountant, because whoever files for her later should be the person who wrote the rows in the first place.
A bookkeeper, but only after an accountant has been paid to clear the backlog and hand over clean books.

quiz.explanation: The work she is describing is bookkeeping: rows kept current, documents matched to them, months closed, a file somebody else could pick up. It is regular, and it costs less per hour. An accountant works on top of records that already exist, on what her situation requires and what to file, so hiring one to clear a backlog is paying senior rates for junior work. Nothing here needs a licensed opinion yet. The moment one arrives, a letter she does not understand or a new client abroad, is the moment to book the accountant, and by then the books will be worth showing.

quiz.prompt: A question has sat in Sheryl's not yet confirmed column since January. She sent it to one person then and it is now September with no reply. Next quarter's decision depends on the answer. What should she do with the row?

options.text: Leave it where it is, since an unanswered question is exactly what that column was built to hold.
Act on the figure that several of the sources online agree on, noting she could not confirm it herself.
Delete the row and raise it again if the decision really does come up, so that the column stays short and current.
Ask a second source, write the date of that second attempt beside the question, and leave the row where it is.

quiz.explanation: The column is a list of open questions, not a place questions go to rest. A row that has sat for eight months is telling her the first attempt failed, and the answer to a failed attempt is another attempt somewhere else, dated so that the next review can see how long this has been running. Leaving it untouched means arriving at the decision with nothing. Deleting it loses the record that she knew the question existed and when she first asked. And acting on what sources happen to agree on is the thing the column exists to stop, whatever she notes beside it.

quiz.prompt: A filing Aldrin has confirmed with his accountant falls due in three weeks. Two things it depends on are not in place: a client owes him a certificate for tax withheld, and a payment document from May was never filed into the month folder. His only reminder is set for the due date itself. What should he change first?

options.text: Nothing, since the date is confirmed and the client will almost certainly send the certificate in time.
Move the reminder several weeks earlier, and start chasing the certificate and the missing document today.
Ask the client for the certificate and, if it has not arrived by the due date, file what he remembers.
File on the due date with whatever he holds, and correct it afterwards once the certificate and the document turn up.

quiz.explanation: The due date is rarely what fails. What fails is everything upstream of it: a certificate sitting in somebody else's inbox, a document that was never filed, an office that is closed, a channel that is down. A reminder arriving on the due date is telling him about a problem he no longer has time to solve, so the reminder moves and the chasing starts now. Filing on a remembered figure puts a number he cannot evidence into something signed in his name. Planning to correct it afterwards accepts that cost before he has even tried to avoid it.

quiz.prompt: Joy has not touched her records since February and it is now July. She has bank and e-wallet statements, a document folder that stops in April, and a client who still owes her a certificate for tax withheld. She has an accountant booked for next week. What should she bring?

options.text: A rebuilt ledger covering all five months, filled in from memory wherever the documents do not reach.
A fresh sheet starting in August, since the older months are too far gone to reconstruct usefully now.
Only the months she has documents for, and a note to mention the other months at some later point.
The statements and documents she has, plus a written list of the gaps and what she is chasing.

quiz.explanation: A documented gap is worth more than an invented reconstruction, because an accountant can work with a known hole and cannot detect a plausible guess. Filling months from memory produces figures nobody can defend if they are ever questioned. Holding back the months she cannot evidence wastes the appointment she is paying for and guarantees a second one, whatever she has noted to raise later. Starting fresh in August leaves the earlier months to surface at a worse moment. Bring the statements, the documents, and an honest list of what is missing and who she is chasing.

quiz.prompt: Dennis files and pays an obligation online. He gets a confirmation on screen with a reference number, and an email arrives. Six months later a question comes up about whether that payment was actually made. What should he have done at the time?

options.text: Trusted that the emailed confirmation would still be searchable in his inbox when he needed it.
Saved the confirmation into that month's folder and put the reference number on the ledger row it belongs to.
Taken a photo of the screen and kept it in his phone gallery with the rest of his work photos.
Written the reference number in the notebook where he keeps things he might need later.

quiz.explanation: Proof that money went out to an obligation deserves the same handling as proof that money came in: a named file in the month folder, and the reference recorded on the row it belongs to, so the ledger points at its own evidence. An inbox search depends on the account, the provider and the wording still being findable in six months. A notebook is not connected to the ledger row anyone will actually be looking at. A photo in a general gallery is technically kept and practically lost.

quiz.prompt: Two freelancers build deadline calendars. Sheryl's sheet has one row per obligation with a source column and a date-checked column. Marilou's sheet carries the same dates, typed neatly, with nothing beyond the dates. A year later, what is the practical difference?

options.text: Sheryl can walk down her sheet and see which rows are old enough to be worth rechecking this year.
Marilou's is easier to read at a glance, which matters more than noting where each date came from.
There is no real difference, since both sheets carry exactly the same set of confirmed due dates.
Sheryl's needs rebuilding from scratch each year, while Marilou's can simply be carried forward as it is.

quiz.explanation: Source and date checked are what make a calendar maintainable: they turn the yearly review into a walk down a column instead of a fresh investigation of every row. Readability is not the binding constraint on a short list, and a tidy date with no provenance is a rumour that now looks official. The two sheets are not equivalent, because only one of them can say how old its information is, and only one of them was ever confirmed. And it is Marilou's that needs rebuilding, since she has no way to tell which dates have quietly gone stale.

quiz.prompt: Joy's accountant asks for her total income for the quarter. Her ledger shows one client payment recorded only as the amount that landed in her account, after a platform fee was taken out. Every other row shows gross, deductions and net. What should she do before sending the total?

options.text: Send the total exactly as it stands, and note the platform fee in the covering message to the accountant.
Add the fee back to the total without changing the row, so the figure she sends is at least correct.
Fix the row from the payout document so it shows gross, the fee and net, then total the gross column.
Send both totals, the one with the fee and the one without, and ask the accountant which of them to use.

quiz.explanation: One row recorded differently from the rest means the gross column no longer totals anything real, and a total she cannot trace back to rows is not defensible. A note in the covering message fixes the email and leaves the books wrong for whoever reads them next. Adjusting the total without fixing the row makes the sheet and the figure disagree, which is worse than either alone. Handing over two totals and a question hands over the problem. Repair the row from the payout document, then let the column add itself up.

assignment.title: Books You Could Hand Over
assignment.brief_mdx:
You are handing your books over. Not to us: to a client asking what you billed them last year, to a bank asking what a self-employed applicant earns, or to an accountant you are hiring next month. Build the thing you would hand over, out of your own work.

If you have no freelance income yet, build the same submission for a worked case you label as one at the top: a plausible set of clients, payments and costs, invented on purpose, kept consistent all the way through. The client's identity, the specific amounts and the specific documents are what you are allowed to invent. Part 5's document-type decision and part 7's deadline calendar are not: even inside a worked case, go and look up what currently applies to a self-employed individual in the Philippines, from the BIR's own site or a real conversation with a bookkeeper or accountant, and name that real, dated source. A worked case with an invented deadline calendar does not pass.

Plain text or Markdown, no uploads. Replace client names you cannot share with Client A, Client B. Eight parts.

1. **The boundary.** Which account or wallet holds business money now, how money reaches you personally and on what schedule, the date you drew the line, and what you did about the transactions sitting before that date. If you have not separated anything yet, write the decision you have actually made and the date it takes effect. An intention with no date is not a boundary.

2. **Your categories.** The list you will use, as a short reference list. Add a one-line reason for any category a stranger would not guess from its name.

3. **One month of ledger rows.** A table, at least ten rows, income and expenses both. Every row carries a date, who paid you or who you paid, a plain description, a category from part 2, the amount, and a document reference naming the file or record that backs it.

4. **One payment that arrived short.** In that table, or written out underneath it, take at least one payment where the amount that landed is not the amount you invoiced. Show the invoiced amount, then each deduction on its own named line (a platform service fee, a transfer charge, a currency conversion, an amount a client withheld), then the amount that landed. The arithmetic has to reconcile line by line. Next to each deduction, say where the figure came from: your own bank statement, a payout record, the client's advice. Do not reach for a rate you have not read off a document. If you are working the labelled case, say the figures are invented in the same breath as you use them.

5. **The document register.** For each row, where its backing document actually lives: a folder, a file name, an email thread, a physical folder. Then a short list of the rows whose document is missing or thin, with how you will chase each one and by when. A register that admits gaps is worth more here than one that hides them. Add one more line that is not a row from your table: what you are currently entitled to issue a client when they pay you (a billing statement only, a Sales Invoice, an Official Receipt, some combination), and the real, dated source you checked to know that, even in a worked case.

6. **Your monthly close.** The steps in order, short enough to follow at the end of a tiring week, naming the fixed day of the month it happens. Include how you tick statements against ledger rows, what you do with a statement line that has no row, and how you correct a month you have already closed.

7. **The deadline calendar.** A table with one row per obligation that applies to you, BIR-facing or not, including any contribution you now make yourself.
